<div><p>4) A 400 mm diameter pulley A, mounted on a counter shaft midway between bearings 1200 mm apart, transmits 50 kW power to a machine below it by a flat belt drive. The power is fed to countershaft by another pulley B 300 mm in diameter and mounted at an overhang of 300 mm. The electric motor vertically below pulley B provides power to it. The belts of both the pulleys are vertical and coefficient of friction between belt and pulley surface is 0.3. The countershaft rotates at 560 rpm. Design the shaft taking permissible shear and normal stresses of 45 MPa and 70 MPa. Assume 20 % overloading of shaft. Take Kb = 1.5 and Kt=1.1. Find the diameter of solid shaft. If the shaft is hollow with ratio of inner diameter to outer diameter 0.6, calculate percentage saving in material and increase in radial dimension of shaft.</p></div><div><img src="https://media.cheggcdn.com/study/4a6/4a601089-6589-4100-b2d9-87740ac531e2/Screenshot2024-03-17at2.49.24AM.png"></div></div></div></div></div></div><h3><p><b>
<mark>:: Solution ::</mark>
</b></p></h3><div class="y"><h3><p><b>
<mark>step: 1</mark>
</b></p></h3>`To` design the solid shaft for the given scenario, we need to calculate the torque and bending moment acting on the shaft due to the transmitted power and overloading. Then, we can use these values to determine the required diameter of the shaft based on the permissible shear and normal stresses.</p><p>Given data:</p><p><h3><p><b>
<mark>Explanation: </mark>
</b></p></h3><br><ul><li>Diameter of pulley A (D₁) = 400 mm</li><li>Distance between bearings supporting pulley A (L) = 1200 mm</li><li>Power transmitted (P) = 50 kW</li><li>Diameter of pulley B (D₂) = 300 mm</li><li>Overhang distance (X) = 300 mm</li><li>Coefficient of friction (μ) = 0.3</li><li>Rotational speed of countershaft (N) = 560 rpm</li><li>Permissible shear stress (τ_perm) = 45 MPa</li><li>Permissible normal stress (σ_perm) = 70 MPa</li><li>Safety factor for shear stress (K) = 1.5</li><li>Safety factor for normal stress (K₁) = 1.1</li><li>Overloading factor (F) = 20%</li></ul>Step-by-step solution:</p><p>`1`. Calculate the torque transmitted by pulley A:</p><p>   \[ T = \frac{P \times 60}{2\pi N} \]</p><p>   \[ T = \frac{50 \times 60}{2\pi \times 560} \]</p><p>   \[ T ≈ 0.533 \, \text{kNm} \]</p><p>`2`. Determine the force exerted by the belt on pulley A:</p><p>   \[ F = \frac{T}{r} \]</p><p>   \[ F = \frac{0.533}{0.2} \]  (radius \(r\) = 0.2 m)</p><p>   \[ F ≈ 2.665 \, \text{kN} \]</p><p>`3`. Calculate the tension in the belt:</p><p>   \[ T_1 = T_2 = F \]</p><p>`4`. Determine the torque transmitted by pulley B:</p><p>   \[ T' = T \times e^{\mu \theta} \]</p><p>   \[ \theta = \arcsin{\frac{X}{L}} \]</p><p>   \[ T' = 0.533 \times e^{0.3 \times \arcsin{\frac{0.3}{1.2}}} \]</p><p>   \[ T' ≈ 0.633 \, \text{kNm} \]</p><p>`5`. Calculate the total torque due to overloading:</p><p>   \[ T_{\text{total}} = (1 + F) \times T' \]</p><p>   \[ T_{\text{total}} = (1 + 0.2) \times 0.633 \]</p><p>   \[ T_{\text{total}} ≈ 0.76 \, \text{kNm} \]</p><p><h3><p><b>
<mark>step: 2</mark>
</b></p></h3>`6`. Determine the bending moment on the shaft:</p><p>   \[ M = \frac{T_{\text{total}}}{2} \]</p><p>   \[ M ≈ \frac{0.76}{2} \]</p><p>   \[ M ≈ 0.38 \, \text{kNm} \]</p><p>`7`. Calculate the diameter of the solid shaft using the bending moment:</p><p>   \[ \sigma = \frac{32 M}{\pi d^3} \]</p><p>   \[ d^3 = \frac{32 M}{\pi \sigma} \]</p><p>   \[ d^3 = \frac{32 \times 0.38}{\pi \times \frac{70}{1.1}} \]</p><p>   \[ d^3 ≈ 53.41 \]</p><p>   \[ d ≈ 4.2 \, \text{cm} \]</p><p>`8`. Considering overloading, the final diameter of the solid shaft:</p><p>   \[ d_{\text{final}} = d \times \sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{1 + F}} \]</p><p>   \[ d_{\text{final}} = 4.2 \times \sqrt[3]{\frac{1}{1 + 0.2}} \]</p><p>   \[ d_{\text{final}} ≈ 3.86 \, \text{cm} \]</p><p>So, the diameter of the solid shaft required is approximately \(3.86 \, \text{cm}\).</p><p>`Now`, let's calculate the percentage saving in material and the increase in radial dimension of the hollow shaft.</p><p>`9`. Calculate the inner diameter of the hollow shaft:</p><p>   \[ d_{\text{inner}} = 0.6 \times d_{\text{final}} \]</p><p>   \[ d_{\text{inner}} = 0.6 \times 3.86 \]</p><p>   \[ d_{\text{inner}} ≈ 2.316 \, \text{cm} \]</p><p>`10`. Calculate the material saved by using a hollow shaft:</p><p>   \[ \text{Material Saved} = \frac{\pi}{4} \times (d_{\text{final}}^2 - d_{\text{inner}}^2) \]</p><p>   \[ \text{Material Saved} = \frac{\pi}{4} \times ((3.86)^2 - (2.316)^2) \]</p><p>   \[ \text{Material Saved} ≈ 8.01 \, \text{cm}^2 \]</p><p>`11`. Calculate the percentage saving in material:</p><p>   \[ \text{Percentage Material Saved} = \frac{\text{Material Saved}}{\pi/4 \times (d_{\text{final}})^2} \times 100 \]</p><p>   \[ \text{Percentage Material Saved} = \frac{8.01}{\pi/4 \times (3.86)^2} \times 100 \]</p><p>   \[ \text{Percentage Material Saved} ≈ 51.39\% \]</p><p>`12`. Calculate the increase in radial dimension of the hollow shaft:</p><p>   \[ \text{Increase in Radial Dimension} = \frac{d_{\text{final}} - d_{\text{inner}}}{d_{\text{inner}}} \times 100 \]</p><p>   \[ \text{Increase in Radial Dimension} = \frac{3.86 - 2.316}{2.316} \times 100 \]</p><p>   \[ \text{Increase in Radial Dimension} ≈ 66.25\% \]</p><p>So, using a hollow shaft results in approximately 51.39% saving in material and a radial dimension increase of approximately 66.25%.</p><p><h3><p><b>
<mark>Explanation: </mark>
</b></p></h3>please refer to solution in this step.</p><p><h3><p><b>
<mark>Final Answer</mark>
</b></p></h3>Final Answer:</p><p>Solid Shaft Diameter: \(3.86 \, \text{cm}\)</p><p>Percentage Material Saved with Hollow Shaft: \(51.39\%\)</p><p>Increase in Radial Dimension with Hollow Shaft: \(66.25\%\)</p><p><div class="z"><h2><p><b>
Likes: 0</p><p>Dislikes:  0
